Foxborough Highschool Division Team #2: PMTC Challenge 
 
 
 Plant Wars: Martian Vs. Earth plant progression 
 
There are many variations of plants that botanists can choose to plant; flowers, 
vegetables, and even fruit. Our group wanted to test how well four random plants would grow 
within an “Earth” planter and test these controlled results to a “Martian” soil group. Martian soil 
is known to have unviable properties, as natural soil contains alkaline, a lack of organic nutrients, 
and high concentrations of salts with metallic properties. As science continues to progress, 
research is crucial to decipher how crops can be successfully grown on Mars to make the 
environment suitable for potential crop growth in the future. 
In this plant experiment, our group has gathered data that tested vegetables and flowers 
that could potentially be grown on Mars, in which we used Cucumber, Zinnia, Sunflower, and 
Lettuce and attempted to measure the success of their growth within both a Martain soil mixture 
(Experimental) and Earth soil group (Control). Although our group had no prior 
acknowledgements of which crop could potentially succeed the most within our experimental 
group, we noted that this experiment could identify and compare which seeds could successful 
when Martian soil is proportioned with a viable soil mixture. The data that we collected with the 
randomized seeds could progress our knowledge of how Martian soil can become viable for 
planting, in which scientists can become closer to solving how the high concentrations of 
alkaline and metals can be combatted to make Mars sustain bio-life. 
 Experimental Design & Variables: 
 
Throughout the entirety of our project, we monitored our plant growth within our 
school’s greenhouse. We began our project by creating planters for both our Martian soil plants 
and earth plants. Our control group within the experiment was our earth group, in which we used 
a composition of 50% compost and 50% planter soil to compare to our Martian experimental 
group. Our Martian soil contained a 50% composition of planter soil alongside the 50% sample 
of Martian soil sample. 
To ensure the experiment exercised consistent variables, our group decided to plant the 
same variations of seeds in both the control and experimental soil, which we decided to plant 4 
cucumber seeds, 4 Zinnia seeds, 8 lettuce seeds, and 4 sunflower seeds in both groups for 
equivalent quantities of seeds. Because lettuce seeds are very small, our group decided to 
amplify the quantity of seeds we would use to attempt to sprout lettuce in both groups. Our crops

would obtain solar energy within the greenhouse throughout our experiment, as well as the 
consistency with watering, which was done every class period and a day prior if we dropped for 
the weekend. 
Our group's initial hypothesis was that if we planted a variety of seeds within Martian soil 
and earth soil, then we would see a trend in which certain crops grew better in the Martian soil. 
Within this experiment, our independent variable was the growth in centimeters of each of our 
plants, which depended on the number of days we conducted this experiment with our resources 
such as water, solar energy, and nutrient quantity within the compost and soil mixtures. 
 
 Procedure: 
 
 We added a 50% composition of Martian and Earth soil to four pots. A few days later we 
placed the seeds in each pot. The seeds we used were Sunflowers, Zinnias, Cucumbers, and 
Lettuce. We tried to sprout and germinate the seeds in wet paper towels before placing them in 
the soil. We watered the seeds every class. At the beginning we added 10 milliliters of water, but 
it changed in the middle of the project because of overwatering to 5 milliliters. We recorded 
videos and wrote down observations during class based on each plant's growth. When the plants 
started to grow, we measured their heights in centimeters. When the plants got taller, we started 
using sticks to support them around week 6. At the end of the experiment, we pulled the roots out 
to see what those looked like and how long they were. 
 
 Qualitative Data Results: 
We kept track of how tall our plants had been growing each day. The sunflowers looked 
and grew the best, especially the Mars one which grew the tallest at 30 centimeters and had a 
purple stem towards the bottom of it. The sunflowers in the Earth's soil looked like normal 
sunflowers. When the sunflowers first grew, the Mars one was 2.5 cm and the Earth ones were 
both 2 cm, at the end the Mars was 30 cm and the Earth ones were 10 cm and 11.5 cm.

Throughout the experiment, there was a noticeable difference in which crops 
progressively grew in terms of centimeters, and some plants did not sprout at all. We 
continued to track all crops within the greenhouse on the same rotating days in our 
Environmental Sustainability class, and after the duration of 8 weeks, we noticed that our 
most successful plant varied between our Control group and Experimental group. Our 
final measurements were the following after data had been collected all eight weeks: ​
Mars sunflower grew to 30 centimeters, Earth soil grew a sunflower to 11.5 centimeters, 
Earth’s Zinnia grew 12 centimeters, Mar’s cucumber grew 12 centimeters. The lettuce for 
both the control and experimental group never sprouted for our group. After the trial of 
growing each plant, our group also documented the root length of every successful plant, 
in which we recorded the following: 9 centimeters for our Martian sunflower, our 
Martian zinnia roots were 3.5 centimeters, Earth sunflowers roots were 4 centimeters in 
length, and our Martian cucumber had roots lengthed at 3 centimeters. From the entirety 
of this experiment, we had fluctuation within our plant growth, but after the 8 weeks in 
total our group has concluded that Sunflower had the most successful growth within a 
Martian soil composition; which grew over 30 centimeters in length. 
 
 Discussion and Conclusion:​
 
 
After the experiment was conducted, it was documented that lettuce did not grow 
in either the experimental or control group, and cucumber did not sprout within our 
control group. Within our experimental group, we witnessed a fluctuation in which 
certain seeds grew taller than others. Our Sunflower for our experimental group grew 
more than 30 centimeters long, its Zinnia planter grew 4 centimeters long while the 
cucumber sprouted to 12 centimeters long. Within our control group, its Sunflower grew 
to 11.5 centimeters Zinnia grew 12 centimeters. Based on this experiment, we can 
conclude that Sunflower was the most successful plant within a composition of 50% soil 
and compost, and 50% soil and Martian sample. 
 
Because temperature, the daylight cycle, potential insects with our planters, and 
our weekend rotations may have altered the quality of our experiment, it’s not cohesive 
enough to measure the exact success rate of each individual seed we had planted in both 
the control and experimental group. Because lettuce did not sprout in both groups, we 
cannot conclude any observations or findings of how successful the growth would be on a 
martin terrain and soil mixture. Our cucumber within our experimental group did not 
sprout accordingly, but the cucumber seedlings within our experimental group grew to 12 
centimeters, revealing inconsistences that doesn't enable us to draw comparisons based 
off the initial Earth soil mixture.

Because our experiment had multiple variables that interfered with results and 
possible conclusions, our group has reflected on how we could've improved this 
experiment. We live in a northern climate where weather and temperature often fluctuate, 
and gets colder at night as fall is beginning to conclude, which is why our group would've 
grown t5he plants in a room temperature environment with an artificial light source if we 
started over; to ensure our plants did not become too cold in the greenhouse at night. We 
would also minimize the amount of water we used for plants, as we saw our crops 
become too overhydrated during week 5 of our plant experiment. With the 
implementation of these variables, we could have had better results to fully measure the 
success of each seed within the control and experimental soils.
